subject: physics
title: Momentum, impulse and force
key_idea: Momentum is mass × velocity, and it has a direction. A resultant force changes momentum, and the force equals the rate of change of momentum. The change in momentum is the impulse, which is the area under a force–time graph.

blocks.text: This section defines momentum and shows why its direction matters.

items.meaning: The product of an object's mass and its velocity.
A quantity with both size and direction.

blocks.label: Linear momentum
where: p = momentum, in kg m/s (or N s)

items: Momentum is a **vector**. It points in the same direction as the velocity.
In one dimension, choose one direction as positive. Momentum in the opposite direction is negative.
A heavy, slow object and a light, fast object can have the same momentum.
Momentum = mass × velocity, measured in kg m/s.
Momentum is a vector, so its sign shows its direction.

sections.heading: Force as rate of change of momentum

blocks.text: A resultant force changes an object's momentum. The bigger the force, the faster the momentum changes.

blocks.label: Force as rate of change of momentum
where: Δp = change in momentum, in kg m/s

items: This is Newton's second law in its general form.
If the mass is constant, Δ(mv) = mΔv. Then F = mΔv / Δt = **ma**.
So F = ma is a special case of F = Δp / Δt, for a constant mass.
The force is in the same direction as the change in momentum.
Resultant force = rate of change of momentum.
F = ma is the special case where the mass stays constant.

blocks.text: Rearranging F = Δp / Δt gives the impulse of a force.

items.meaning: The force multiplied by the time it acts. It equals the change in momentum.

blocks.label: Impulse
where: Δt = time the force acts, in s
Δp = change in momentum, in kg m/s (or N s)

items: On a force–time graph, the **area under the line** is the impulse.
The area is therefore the change in momentum.
For a force that changes with time, split the area into rectangles and triangles, or count squares.
For a curved graph, estimate the area, for example by counting squares.

diagram.alt: A slider showing a car stopping in a crash. Changing the contact time changes the average force while the change in momentum stays the same.

items: For the same change in momentum, a **longer contact time** gives a smaller average force.
Crumple zones, air bags, padding and packaging all lengthen the contact time.
A kicked football is the opposite case: a short contact time means a large force.
Impulse = FΔt = change in momentum.
The area under a force–time graph is the impulse.
A longer contact time reduces the force for the same change in momentum.

checks.q: A 0.15 kg ball is moving at 20 m/s. Calculate its momentum.
checks.a: p = mv = 0.15 × 20 = 3.0 kg m/s, in the direction of motion.

checks.q: A force of 40 N acts on a trolley for 0.25 s. State the impulse and the change in momentum of the trolley.
checks.a: Impulse = FΔt = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N s. The change in momentum is equal to the impulse, 10 kg m/s.

checks.q: Explain, using momentum, why an air bag reduces the force on a driver in a crash.
checks.a: The driver's momentum changes by the same amount to reach zero. The air bag increases the time over which this happens. Force = rate of change of momentum, so the average force is smaller.

items: Quantitative questions can use forces that **vary with time**. Find the impulse from the area under the force–time graph.
Impact forces depend on contact times. Examples are kicking a football, crumple zones and packaging.
Be ready to discuss momentum and ethical transport design. Lengthening the stopping time of a vehicle reduces the force on its passengers.
Elastic and inelastic collisions and explosions are covered in the note on conservation of momentum.
You must be able to **define** momentum: the product of mass and velocity.
You must be able to **define** force: the rate of change of momentum.
Use both definitions to solve problems, not only to state them.
Be able to **estimate the area** under a non-linear force–time graph, for example by counting squares.
A spreadsheet can find the impulse from force–time data. Multiply each force by its time interval, then add the results.
Know that F = ma is a special case of net force = Δp / Δt.
